candidates.title: InteractiveWorld: A Verifiable Human-Centric Environment for Building Better Interactive MLLM Assistants
candidates.content: People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user's physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today's MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. candidates.title: World-in-Context: Interactive Video World Modeling with In-Context Conditioning
candidates.content: Interactive video world models require coordinated control over viewing perspectives, character actions, and camera motion. Existing methods typically leave view modes implicit in text captions, conflate action with camera motion, and inject controls through fragmented architectural pathways that capture interdependencies only indirectly. In this work, we present World-in-Context, an interactive world modeling framework powered by In-Context Conditioning (ICC). Rather than relying on specialized conditioning pathways, World-in-Context unifies view, action, and camera controls into explicit tokens contextualized directly within a shared self-attention space. Our formulation reveals that (i) explicit view tokens disentangle conflicting dynamics and unlock emergent view switching from single-view data, while (ii) action and camera inputs play complementary roles in governing local responsiveness and global stability. To preserve temporal continuity across execution intervals, we further introduce Interaction-Transport RoPE (IT-RoPE), parameterizing temporal attention with accumulated control transitions. candidates.title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution
candidates.content: LLM agents are increasingly used to solve real-world problems, and their effectiveness depends on both the underlying models and the harnesses that support their operation. However, most existing benchmarks focus on model capabilities and overall agent performance, with limited attention to the evaluation of agent harnesses. To address this gap, we introduce TraceTrial-Bench, which organizes harness reliability into seven components covering context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. We construct 95 expert-level, mechanism-oriented tasks with executable or state-based ground truth to support semantically equivalent comparisons while preserving the native behavior of each harness. We design a Trajectory Tracing (TT) module to capture agent execution traces and introduce a two-layer evaluation framework that separately assesses agent performance and harness reliability. candidates.title: Structural basis for coupled DNA replication and uracil repair by a family of DNA polymerases from phages with T-modified genomes
candidates.content: Abstract Replicative DNA polymerases (DNAPs) play a critical role in genome duplication, ensuring the accurate transmission of genetic information in all domains of life. DNAPs are also essential for DNA viruses, as well as bacteriophages, where a uracil-DNA glycosylase (UDG) is often encoded in trans or is present in the DNAP gene. Here, we identify a new group of A-family DNAPs in phages that are fused to an active UDG domain and contain other large insertions. Several members of this subfamily, including phages SP-15 and YerA41, are known to be hypermodified on their thymidine base through glycosylation of a linker attached to the C5 position of thymine. We determined the atomic cryo-EM structures for two of its members in various active functional and conformational states, from YerA41 and phiLo phages. The structures reveal how these large DNAPs function as replicative DNAPs, and how they can recognize dU bases ahead of the replication fork through their UDG domain, generating abasic sites that are preferentially bypassed through dA incorporation. Such dU errors would need to be eliminated to preserve phage genome integrity. Additionally, we report the co-occurrence of both an

candidates.title: Neuronal DNA repair mediates systemic mitochondrial maintenance through acetylcholine signaling
candidates.content: Abstract DNA repair defects such as nucleotide excision repair (NER) mutations can lead to progeroid syndromes characterized by growth retardation and accelerated aging with distinct tissue type specific pathologies. DNA-damage-induced dysfunction of specific cell types can impair the organism’s overall function. It is unknown whether, in reverse, DNA repair in specific tissues can have non-cell-autonomous consequences on other tissues carrying DNA damage. To explore the organismal consequences of cell-type-specific DNA repair, we restricted NER activity to specific tissues and monitored consequences on organismal health in Caenorhabditis elegans . Unexpectedly, we observed that tissue-specific DNA repair is sufficient to improve overall DNA damage resistance. Strikingly, NER activity restricted to neurons only is sufficient to provide similar overall DNA damage resistance as whole-body NER in almost all tissues tested. We show that this systemic DNA damage resilience is mediated by neuronal acetylcholine signaling that promotes the maintenance of mitochondrial activity throughout the organism.

candidates.title: Polymorphic Structures of an Artificial Nucleocapsid Evolved from a Circularly Permuted Bacterial Protein Cage
candidates.content: Molecular self-assembly provides a route to nanoscale structures with defined sizes and shapes. Protein cages assembled from repeated subunits form compartments that can package molecular cargoes. Although amino acid substitutions can alter intersubunit interactions and cage architecture, how protein backbone connectivity relates to the cage architectures accessible during laboratory evolution remains unclear. Here we evolved an artificial nucleocapsid from a circularly permuted variant of Aquifex aeolicus lumazine synthase (AaLS). Laboratory evolution increased the yield of purified nucleocapsids relative to the progenitor, and the evolved variant, NC119-3, packaged its encoding mRNA. Cryo-electron microscopy revealed a heterogeneous population of cages, within which we resolved 180- and 210-subunit cage families composed of 36 and 42 pentamers, respectively. Within each resolved family, particles with the same subunit stoichiometry differed in the arrangement and orientation of their pentameric building blocks. candidates.content: arXiv:2610.31673v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Forecasting pandemic spread across heterogeneous regions demands models that are both accurate and interpretable for public health action. This paper proposes a hybrid forecasting framework that integrates an SEIR epidemiological model enhanced with a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) to produce interpretable multi-horizon infection forecasts. Using region-wise COVID-19 data from the Our World in Data corpus, we present a unified pipeline that integrates epidemiological indicators (susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered), intervention signals (masking, vaccination, policies), mobility covariates, and demographic context. The SEIR component estimates latent disease dynamics and injects mechanistic priors, while the TFT learns non-linear temporal dependencies and cross-feature interactions from historical observations and known future inputs. To ensure transparency, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) is applied at both global and local levels, quantifying feature contributions and revealing region-specific drivers of surges and slowdowns. candidates.title: Decoupling candidate dual AGN from chance superpositions in the GOTHIC survey via a deep-learning framework
candidates.content: arXiv:2608.24164v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dual active galactic nuclei (DAGN) mark a critical phase in the evolution of merging galaxies and the pairing of supermassive black holes, yet they remain difficult to identify in large imaging surveys because of projection effects and limited spatial resolution. Compact foreground stars and unresolved substructure can mimic dual nuclei through chance superposition, complicating automated detection. We revisit the 46,061 galaxies flagged but rejected as DAGN candidates by the GOTHIC pipeline, primarily because the two nuclei fell within the SDSS fibre aperture or exceeded its separation threshold. We train a supervised deep-learning framework based on the YOLOv11 oriented-bounding-box architecture on annotated SDSS imaging to separate genuine dual nuclei from foreground stellar contaminants and other spurious alignments. candidates.title: Continual Learning Exam: Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents
candidates.content: Continual learning is the ability of LLM agents to improve over time by acquiring, refining, and applying knowledge from experience while retaining useful prior knowledge. It is essential for agents learning over long time horizons, yet current evaluations largely assess individual task performance rather than improvement through accumulated experience. We introduce Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale benchmark developed by 50+ domain experts to measure experience-driven improvement in realistic professional workflows. CLE comprises 120 human-authored tasks, each organised as a five-level ladder, yielding 600 levels spanning 89 professional roles across 12 occupational domains. Agents must pass each level to unlock the next, with later levels building on experience accumulated during earlier assignments. An evaluation agent assesses each submission against human-authored rubrics. We compare a single-submission setting with one that provides diagnostic feedback after failure and allows one revision. candidates.title: Profile-Driven User Simulation via Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Rewards for Task-Oriented Dialogues
candidates.content: arXiv:2610.32435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building Task-Oriented Dialogue (TOD) systems for high-value scenarios such as financial marketing requires large volumes of domain-specific dialogue data, which privacy regulations, annotation costs, and the need for expert labor make hard to obtain. User simulation offers a remedy, but existing methods target general-domain dialogue and exhibit two key limitations: insufficient modeling of domain-specific business processes and compliance constraints, and inadequate capture of the colloquial, spoken-language character of voice interactions. We propose ProfileSim, a profile-driven user simulation framework for financial marketing outbound calls. It jointly models user profiles---demographics and Big Five personality traits---and business profiles---intents reverse-engineered from real call logs---enabling fine-grained control over simulated behavior. The base model is fine-tuned on real voice dialogue data and refined by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with hierarchical rewards at the dialogue and utterance levels. candidates.title: Frontier-OPD: Discovering the Edge of Agent Capability and Teaching Agents to Go Beyond
candidates.content: arXiv:2610.32802v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy distillation aligns teacher feedback with a student's current behavior, yet acquiring useful supervision for multi-turn agents requires identifying both where guidance is needed and whether the student can sustain the interaction afterward. We introduce Frontier-OPD, which addresses this problem through the student's learning frontier: decision situations that remain challenging but admit useful autonomous continuation after brief teacher guidance. To operationalize this frontier, Frontier-OPD organizes on-policy experience into a shared-state trajectory graph, where trajectory-balanced aggregation of teacher-student disagreement identifies distinct intervention candidates while preserving the histories needed for replay. Short teacher bridges are then assessed by comparing agreement over the bridge and the ensuing student continuation with an equally long segment of the original trajectory, providing a behavioral proxy for guidance that the current student can build on. candidates.title: InferSlice: A Reference Architecture for SLO-driven LLM Inference over a Telco Wide-Area Network
candidates.content: arXiv:2610.32638v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM inference is increasingly deployed as a core service for enterprise and interactive applications, but sovereignty, compliance, latency and resource-locality requirements can limit the suitability of centralised cloud deployments. Telco operators offer geographically distributed compute and network infrastructure for addressing these constraints. However, existing LLM serving frameworks are designed for tightly coupled data centres and provide limited support for coordinating geographically distributed and heterogeneous resources. We present InferSlice, a reference architecture for Service-Level Objective (SLO)-driven LLM inference over a telco infrastructure, integrating network slicing, GPU partitioning, elastic serving and observability. candidates.title: Interchangeable in Role, Not in History: Replacing Members of Formed LLM Teams
candidates.content: arXiv:2609.05279v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multiagent LLM systems often treat a role as a slot: when a member is replaced, any agent competent at the role is expected to fill it. We test this view on teams whose members keep short written notebooks. A one-seat swap replays a formed, frozen team with its own member, with a same-role newcomer carrying another team's notebook for that role, or with a newcomer carrying none. In cooperative cooking, wildfire response and medical question answering, the experienced newcomer, averaged over seats, outscores the one without a notebook in every setting, so the usual comparison would approve it. Against the original team, the same replacement falls short in every setting, and the team spends more messages per unit of progress. On the hardest cooking level, the shortfall appears only after the team has worked together, persists across model families and decoding temperatures, and narrows by two thirds with added planning-only members.
